items.stem: What is a tariff?
options: A limit on the quantity of imports
items.answer: A tax on imported goods
items.markingKey: Raises the price of imports.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a tariff and a quota.
items.answer: A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price and earns revenue; a quota is a limit on the quantity imported, which raises the domestic price but earns the government no revenue (unless licences are sold).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: tariff tax/price/revenue; 1 mark: quota quantity limit/no revenue [2]

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a diagram, how a tariff affects domestic production and imports.
items.answer: The tariff raises the domestic price from Pw to Pw + t; domestic quantity supplied rises along the supply curve, quantity demanded falls, so imports (the gap) fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price rises by tariff; 1 mark: domestic output rises; 1 mark: demand falls and imports fall [3]

items.stem: Kestria prohibits imports of electric scooters from Rovania for five years. Which method of protection is this?
items.answer: Embargo
items.markingKey: Embargo: a ban on imports of a product from a country.

items.stem: The government of Quentara adds a 25% tax to the price of imported washing machines. Which method of protection is this? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Tariff: a tax on imports raises their price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Tariff; 1 mark: explanation – a tax on imports raises their price. [2]

items.stem: Identify the method of protection in each case and explain how it protects domestic producers. (i) Umbria Nova requires all imported running shoes to pass lengthy safety tests that domestic products do not face. (ii) Umbria Nova limits imports of running shoes to 50,000 units a year.
items.answer: (i) Administrative barrier (ii) Quota
items.markingKey: (i) Administrative barrier – red tape and standards that make importing costly or slow. [2] (ii) Quota – a physical limit on the quantity imported. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of cement in Tarvia say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Dravonia, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $8, domestic firms supply 50 thousand units and consumers buy 126 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $6 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 80 thousand and cut consumption to 90 thousand. Economists warn that Dravonia might retaliate against Tarvia’s exports of chocolate bars. (a) Calculate the change in imports caused by the tariff. (b) Explain what is meant by dumping.
items.answer: (a) Before 76 thousand, after 10 thousand: a fall of 66 thousand. (b) Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Before 76 thousand, after 10 thousand: a fall of 66 thousand. [2] (b) Credit: Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of furniture in Tarvia say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Fendaria, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $6, domestic firms supply 17 thousand units and consumers buy 61 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $3 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 23 thousand and cut consumption to 43 thousand. Economists warn that Fendaria might retaliate against Tarvia’s exports of laptops. (a) Calculate the tariff revenue. (b) Using a diagram, explain the effect of the tariff on consumers and domestic producers.
items.answer: (a) $3 × 20 thousand = $60,000. (b) Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $3 × 20 thousand = $60,000. [1] (b) Credit: Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles. [4]

items.stem: What is an import quota?
options: A physical limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
items.answer: A physical limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
items.markingKey: Restricts quantity, not price directly.

items.stem: Explain why a production subsidy may be a less harmful form of protection than a tariff.
items.answer: Consumers still pay the world price, so consumption is not reduced; the cost is borne by taxpayers and is visible, though it has an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: consumers still pay world price; 1 mark: cost to taxpayers/opportunity cost [2]

items.stem: Explain how administrative barriers can act as protection even though they are not taxes.
items.answer: Paperwork, inspections and special standards raise foreign firms’ costs and delay imports, discouraging them in favour of domestic goods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: raise costs/delays for importers; 1 mark: favour domestic producers [2]

items.stem: Zentara limits imports of televisions to 50,000 units a year. Which method of protection is this?
items.answer: Quota
items.markingKey: Quota: a physical limit on the quantity imported.

items.stem: The government of Nordavia is under pressure from domestic producers to restrict imports. Explain the different methods of protection a government could use to reduce imports.
items.answer: Tariffs, quotas, embargoes, subsidies to domestic producers, administrative barriers, exchange controls; how each works.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Tariffs, quotas, embargoes, subsidies to domestic producers, administrative barriers, exchange controls; how each works. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of bicycles in Selmaria say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Umbria Nova, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $6, domestic firms supply 23 thousand units and consumers buy 73 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $2 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 29 thousand and cut consumption to 69 thousand. Economists warn that Umbria Nova might retaliate against Selmaria’s exports of steel pipes. (a) Explain what is meant by dumping. (b) Explain one reason why retaliation would harm the economy.
items.answer: (a) Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. (b) Exports of steel pipes fall, reducing income, jobs and the current account.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. [2] (b) Credit: Exports of steel pipes fall, reducing income, jobs and the current account. [2]

items.stem: Unemployment in the industrial regions of Selmaria is above 12%. To what extent do you agree that subsidies to domestic producers are the least harmful form of protection?
items.answer: For: Consumers still pay the world price; targeted; no deadweight loss on consumption. Against: Opportunity cost of public funds, taxes needed; may be challenged under WTO rules; still inefficiency in production; judgement. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Consumers still pay the world price; targeted; no deadweight loss on consumption. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Opportunity cost of public funds, taxes needed; may be challenged under WTO rules; still inefficiency in production; judgement. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: What is the infant industry argument for protection?
options: Children’s goods should be exempt from tariffs
Old industries should be protected permanently
New industries need temporary protection until they are large enough to compete
All industries need protection from imports
items.answer: New industries need temporary protection until they are large enough to compete
items.markingKey: Grow to achieve economies of scale.

items.stem: Explain the infant industry argument for protection.
items.answer: New firms have high average costs because they are small and inexperienced; temporary protection lets them grow, gain economies of scale and learning, and then compete internationally, after which protection should be removed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: high costs of new firms; 1 mark: grow/economies of scale; 1 mark: temporary [3]

items.stem: Explain why a country might protect its industries against dumping.
items.answer: Dumped goods sold below cost can drive efficient domestic firms out of business; foreign firms may then raise prices once competition is removed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: below-cost price harms domestic firms; 1 mark: threat of later monopoly pricing/unfair competition [2]

items.stem: The government of Loristan uses tariffs because it has difficulty collecting income tax. Which argument for protection is being used?
items.answer: Raising government revenue
items.markingKey: Raising government revenue: tariffs are easy to collect at the border.

items.stem: Nordavia uses import tariffs to reduce a large current account deficit. Which argument for protection is being used? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correcting a current account deficit: lower imports reduce the deficit, at least in the short run.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Correcting a current account deficit; 1 mark: explanation – lower imports reduce the deficit, at least in the short run. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of washing machines in Dravonia say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Pelora, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $6, domestic firms supply 35 thousand units and consumers buy 85 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $1 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 40 thousand and cut consumption to 80 thousand. Economists warn that Pelora might retaliate against Dravonia’s exports of furniture. (a) Calculate the change in imports caused by the tariff. (b) Explain what is meant by dumping.
items.answer: (a) Before 50 thousand, after 40 thousand: a fall of 10 thousand. (b) Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Before 50 thousand, after 40 thousand: a fall of 10 thousand. [2] (b) Credit: Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. [2]

items.stem: What is meant by dumping?
options: Selling goods abroad at a price below cost or below the price in the home market
Disposing of waste products in another country
Selling goods at a high price abroad
items.answer: Selling goods abroad at a price below cost or below the price in the home market
items.markingKey: Unfair competition.

items.stem: Explain two arguments for protection that a low-income country might use.
items.answer: Infant industry (develop new manufacturing); revenue (tariffs easy to collect); protecting employment; diversification away from primary exports; strategic food security.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two arguments, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: A tariff on imported solar panels in Selmaria raises consumers’ spending on solar panels by $200m a year and is estimated to save 2,000 jobs in domestic factories. The average wage in the industry is $18,000 a year. Calculate the cost to consumers of each job saved.

Identify the argument for protection in each case and explain it. (i) The government of Lunaria uses tariffs because it has difficulty collecting income tax. (ii) Lunaria uses import tariffs to reduce a large current account deficit.
items.answer: (i) Raising government revenue (ii) Correcting a current account deficit
items.markingKey: (i) Raising government revenue – tariffs are easy to collect at the border. [2] (ii) Correcting a current account deficit – lower imports reduce the deficit, at least in the short run. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Which is an argument against protection?
options: It may lead to retaliation by other countries
items.answer: It may lead to retaliation by other countries
items.markingKey: Trade wars reduce exports.

items.stem: Explain how protection can lead to a misallocation of resources.
items.answer: It keeps resources in high-cost domestic industries where the country lacks comparative advantage, rather than moving them to more efficient uses; world output is lower.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources in comparative-disadvantage industries; 1 mark: lower total/world output [2]

items.stem: Explain two consequences of a trade war for a country’s economy.
items.answer: Exports fall as partners retaliate, reducing output and employment in export industries; import prices rise, raising inflation and costs of inputs; lower growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two consequences, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: World trade falls as several countries raise tariffs at the same time. Which consequence of protectionism does this illustrate?
options: Higher prices and less choice for consumers
items.answer: Lower world output and trade
items.markingKey: Lower world output and trade: gains from specialisation are lost.

items.stem: Car makers in Pelora face higher costs after tariffs are imposed on imported steel. Which consequence of protectionism does this illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Higher costs for firms using imported inputs: protection raises input costs and lowers competitiveness.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Higher costs for firms using imported inputs; 1 mark: explanation – protection raises input costs and lowers competitiveness. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of laptops in Ostrelia say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Korvia, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $8, domestic firms supply 32 thousand units and consumers buy 96 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $6 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 56 thousand and cut consumption to 66 thousand. Economists warn that Korvia might retaliate against Ostrelia’s exports of bicycles. (a) Calculate the change in imports caused by the tariff. (b) Explain what is meant by dumping.
items.answer: (a) Before 64 thousand, after 10 thousand: a fall of 54 thousand. (b) Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Before 64 thousand, after 10 thousand: a fall of 54 thousand. [2] (b) Credit: Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. [2]

items.stem: Explain why protection may not improve the current account in the long run.
items.answer: Retaliation reduces exports; higher input costs and lower efficiency reduce export competitiveness; the currency may appreciate as imports fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: retaliation/exports fall; 1 mark: competitiveness falls [2]

items.stem: Kwame makes the following statement: ‘Protection has no effect on other countries.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Foreign exporters lose sales and income, and may persuade their governments to retaliate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Foreign exporters lose sales and income, and may persuade their governments to retaliate. [2]

items.stem: Car makers in Jovania use 1.5 tonnes of imported steel per car, at $800 per tonne. The government imposes a 30% tariff on imported steel. The average car sells for $25,000. Calculate the increase in the steel cost of each car.

Identify the consequence of protection in each case and explain it. (i) World trade falls as several countries raise tariffs at the same time. (ii) Consumers in Ostrelia pay 30% more for televisions after an import quota is introduced. (iii) Protected televisions producers in Ostrelia stop investing in new technology.
items.answer: (i) Lower world output and trade (ii) Higher prices and less choice for consumers (iii) Reduced efficiency and innovation
items.markingKey: (i) Lower world output and trade – gains from specialisation are lost. [2] (ii) Higher prices and less choice for consumers – protection raises prices and reduces consumer surplus. [2] (iii) Reduced efficiency and innovation – without competition, there is less incentive to cut costs. [2] Total [6]

items.stem: What is an embargo?
options: A complete ban on trade in a good or with a country
items.answer: A complete ban on trade in a good or with a country
items.markingKey: The most extreme form of protection.

items.stem: Kenji makes the following statement: ‘A subsidy to domestic producers is not a form of protection because it does not affect imports.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Subsidies lower domestic firms’ costs and prices, so domestic output replaces imports; this protects domestic producers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Subsidies lower domestic firms’ costs and prices, so domestic output replaces imports; this protects domestic producers. [2]

items.stem: A student, Zara, claims: ‘A quota raises revenue for the government in the same way as a tariff.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: A quota limits quantity; the higher price benefits licence holders or foreign exporters, so the government earns no revenue unless it sells import licences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A quota limits quantity; the higher price benefits licence holders or foreign exporters, so the government earns no revenue unless it sells import licences. [2]

items.stem: In Jovania, the domestic demand for washing machines is Qd = 86 − 4P and domestic supply is Qs = 5 + 4P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands of units a year. Jovania can import any quantity at the world price of $6. The government imposes a tariff of $1 per unit. Calculate the quantity imported after the tariff.
items.answer: 25 thousand units
items.markingKey: At $7: Qd = 58, Qs = 33; imports = 25 thousand.

items.stem: Dravonia limits imports of steel pipes to 50,000 units a year. Which method of protection is this?
items.answer: Quota
items.markingKey: Quota: a physical limit on the quantity imported.

items.stem: In Jovania, the domestic demand for laptops is Qd = 156 − 4P and domestic supply is Qs = −10 + 5P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands of units a year. Jovania can import any quantity at the world price of $10. The government imposes a tariff of $4 per unit. Calculate the quantity imported after the tariff.
items.answer: 40 thousand units
items.markingKey: At $14: Qd = 100, Qs = 60; imports = 40 thousand.

items.stem: Explain the different methods of protection a government could use to reduce imports.
items.answer: Tariffs, quotas, embargoes, subsidies to domestic producers, administrative barriers, exchange controls; how each works.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Tariffs, quotas, embargoes, subsidies to domestic producers, administrative barriers, exchange controls; how each works. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of steel pipes in Rovania say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Istrana, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $10, domestic firms supply 30 thousand units and consumers buy 112 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $6 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 48 thousand and cut consumption to 88 thousand. Economists warn that Istrana might retaliate against Rovania’s exports of car tyres. (a) Calculate the change in imports caused by the tariff. (b) Explain what is meant by dumping.
items.answer: (a) Before 82 thousand, after 40 thousand: a fall of 42 thousand. (b) Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Before 82 thousand, after 40 thousand: a fall of 42 thousand. [2] (b) Credit: Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. [2]

items.stem: Which is a strategic argument for protection?
options: A country should produce its own food and defence equipment to avoid dependence on others
Imports are always of lower quality
items.answer: A country should produce its own food and defence equipment to avoid dependence on others
items.markingKey: National security.

items.stem: In a revision note Kenji wrote: ‘Protection always saves jobs in Ostrelia overall.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: It may save jobs in protected industries, but jobs can be lost in export industries (retaliation) and in firms using imported inputs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It may save jobs in protected industries, but jobs can be lost in export industries (retaliation) and in firms using imported inputs. [2]

items.stem: During a class discussion Jonas said: ‘Protection always saves jobs in Korvia overall.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: It may save jobs in protected industries, but jobs can be lost in export industries (retaliation) and in firms using imported inputs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – It may save jobs in protected industries, but jobs can be lost in export industries (retaliation) and in firms using imported inputs. [2]

items.stem: A producer in Korvia sells running shoes for $80 per unit in its home market, its average cost is $72, and it sells to Lunaria at $54 per unit. Lunaria sets an anti-dumping duty equal to the difference between the home-market price and the export price. What duty per unit is set?

A tariff on imported car tyres in Dravonia raises consumers’ spending on car tyres by $360m a year and is estimated to save 2,400 jobs in domestic factories. The average wage in the industry is $18,000 a year. (a) Calculate the cost to consumers of each job saved. (b) Compare this with the average wage and comment.
items.answer: (a) $360m / 2,400 = $150,000. (b) This is 8.3 times the average wage, so it would be cheaper to pay the workers’ wages directly or to fund retraining; protection is a costly way to save jobs.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) comparison [1]; comment [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of running shoes in Dravonia say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Lunaria, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $10, domestic firms supply 50 thousand units and consumers buy 79 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $2 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 60 thousand and cut consumption to 75 thousand. Economists warn that Lunaria might retaliate against Dravonia’s exports of furniture. (a) Calculate the tariff revenue. (b) Using a diagram, explain the effect of the tariff on consumers and domestic producers.
items.answer: (a) $2 × 15 thousand = $30,000. (b) Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $2 × 15 thousand = $30,000. [1] (b) Credit: Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles. [4]

items.stem: How does protection affect consumers?
options: They pay higher prices and have less choice
items.answer: They pay higher prices and have less choice
items.markingKey: Consumer surplus falls.

items.stem: Quentara retaliates against Westaria’s tariffs by taxing Westaria’s exports of running shoes. Explain the likely effect on Westaria’s economy.
items.answer: Exports of running shoes fall, reducing output, income and employment in that industry and worsening the current account; the multiplier spreads the effect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: exports fall; 1 mark: effect on income/jobs/current account [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Ethan wrote: ‘Protecting the steel industry in Gorvania will make all manufacturers more competitive.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Firms that use steel face higher input costs, so their competitiveness falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Firms that use steel face higher input costs, so their competitiveness falls. [2]

items.stem: Consumers in Fendaria pay 30% more for paper after an import quota is introduced. Which consequence of protectionism does this illustrate?
options: Higher prices and less choice for consumers
Higher costs for firms using imported inputs
items.answer: Higher prices and less choice for consumers
items.markingKey: Higher prices and less choice for consumers: protection raises prices and reduces consumer surplus.

items.stem: Car makers in Sundara use 1.2 tonnes of imported steel per car, at $900 per tonne. The government imposes a 10% tariff on imported steel. The average car sells for $20,000. (a) Calculate the increase in the steel cost of each car and express it as a percentage of the car price. (b) Explain one effect on the car makers.
items.answer: (a) Extra cost = 1.2 × $900 × 10% = $108 per car, 0.54% of the price. (b) Higher costs reduce profit margins or force higher prices, making exports less competitive.
items.markingKey: (a) cost [1]; percentage [1] (b) [1] [3]

The government is considering a tariff of $6 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 53 thousand and cut consumption to 73 thousand. Economists warn that Calvania might retaliate against Nordavia’s exports of cement. (a) Explain what is meant by dumping. (b) Using a diagram, explain the effect of the tariff on consumers and domestic producers.
items.answer: (a) Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. (b) Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Selling exports at a price below cost or below the home-market price. [2] (b) Credit: Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles. [4]

items.stem: Which method of protection raises revenue for the government?
items.answer: A tariff
items.markingKey: Tariff revenue = tariff per unit × imports.

items.stem: Selmaria replaces its 20% tariff on imported televisions with a quota that allows the same quantity of imports. Explain one difference this makes.
items.answer: The domestic price and quantity of imports may be the same, but the government loses tariff revenue; the gain goes to licence holders or foreign exporters as quota rent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same price/quantity; 1 mark: revenue goes to licence holders not government [2]

items.stem: Quentara replaces its 20% tariff on imported cement with a quota that allows the same quantity of imports. Explain one difference this makes.
items.answer: The domestic price and quantity of imports may be the same, but the government loses tariff revenue; the gain goes to licence holders or foreign exporters as quota rent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same price/quantity; 1 mark: revenue goes to licence holders not government [2]

items.stem: Imports of paper into Dravonia must enter through one small port with slow customs checks. Which method of protection is this?
items.answer: Administrative barrier
items.markingKey: Administrative barrier: bureaucratic procedures raise the cost of importing.

items.stem: In Merania, the domestic demand for electric scooters is Qd = 75 − 2P and domestic supply is Qs = 10 + 3P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands of units a year. Merania can import any quantity at the world price of $6. The government imposes a tariff of $3 per unit. Calculate the quantity imported after the tariff.
items.answer: 20 thousand units
items.markingKey: At $9: Qd = 57, Qs = 37; imports = 20 thousand.

items.stem: The government of Korvia pays domestic bicycles producers $15 per unit produced. Which method of protection is this?
items.answer: Subsidy to domestic producers
items.markingKey: Subsidy to domestic producers: lowers domestic firms’ costs so they can compete with imports.

items.stem: Why might a developing country use tariffs to raise revenue?
options: Tariffs are paid by foreign governments
Tariffs are easier to collect than income tax
Tariffs have no effect on prices
items.answer: Tariffs are easier to collect than income tax
items.markingKey: Few collection points at borders.

items.stem: Umbria Nova wants to develop a domestic paper industry. Explain why it might use protection, and what conditions would make this successful.
items.answer: Infant industry: temporary protection while firms grow and gain economies of scale. It works only if protection is time-limited, firms invest and become efficient, and there is a real potential comparative advantage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: infant industry; 1 mark: condition (temporary/potential CA/investment) [2]

items.stem: Foreign firms are selling laptops in Merania at prices below what they charge at home. Explain why Merania might impose an anti-dumping duty.
items.answer: Below-cost imports may drive efficient domestic producers out; the duty restores fair competition and prevents a later foreign monopoly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: unfair competition/harm to domestic firms; 1 mark: duty restores fair price [2]

items.stem: Istrana gives temporary protection to its coal industry while workers retrain. Which argument for protection is being used?
items.answer: Protecting a declining industry
items.markingKey: Protecting a declining industry: slows the pace of structural change to reduce unemployment.

items.stem: A tariff on imported car tyres in Istrana raises consumers’ spending on car tyres by $200m a year and is estimated to save 1,500 jobs in domestic factories. The average wage in the industry is $25,000 a year. (a) Calculate the cost to consumers of each job saved. (b) Compare this with the average wage and comment.
items.answer: (a) $200m / 1,500 = $133,333. (b) This is 5.3 times the average wage, so it would be cheaper to pay the workers’ wages directly or to fund retraining; protection is a costly way to save jobs.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) comparison [1]; comment [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of smartphones in Tarvia say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Fendaria, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $4, domestic firms supply 22 thousand units and consumers buy 49 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $2 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 28 thousand and cut consumption to 43 thousand. Economists warn that Fendaria might retaliate against Tarvia’s exports of televisions. (a) Calculate the change in imports caused by the tariff. (b) Calculate the tariff revenue. (c) Explain one reason why retaliation would harm the economy.
items.answer: (a) Before 27 thousand, after 15 thousand: a fall of 12 thousand. (b) $2 × 15 thousand = $30,000. (c) Exports of televisions fall, reducing income, jobs and the current account.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Before 27 thousand, after 15 thousand: a fall of 12 thousand. [2] (b) Credit: $2 × 15 thousand = $30,000. [1] (c) Credit: Exports of televisions fall, reducing income, jobs and the current account. [2]

items.stem: Why might protection reduce the efficiency of domestic firms?
options: They face higher demand for exports
They face less competition, so have less incentive to cut costs
They must compete harder with imports
They have to pay higher tariffs
items.answer: They face less competition, so have less incentive to cut costs
items.markingKey: X-inefficiency.

items.stem: In a revision note Hana wrote: ‘A tariff makes everyone in Westaria better off because domestic firms sell more.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Producers and the government gain, but consumers lose more than they gain, so there is a net deadweight loss; exporters may lose through retaliation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Producers and the government gain, but consumers lose more than they gain, so there is a net deadweight loss; exporters may lose through retaliation. [2]

items.stem: Westaria imposed a 25% tariff on imported steel pipes five years ago. Domestic producers have not cut costs since then. Explain why.
items.answer: With protection from foreign competition, firms can survive with high costs; there is little incentive to innovate (X-inefficiency) and they may lobby to keep the tariff.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reduced competition; 1 mark: no incentive to cut costs/X-inefficiency [2]

items.stem: Car makers in Halvoria use 1.2 tonnes of imported steel per car, at $900 per tonne. The government imposes a 10% tariff on imported steel. The average car sells for $25,000. Calculate the increase in the steel cost of each car.

Car makers in Dravonia use 1.2 tonnes of imported steel per car, at $800 per tonne. The government imposes a 25% tariff on imported steel. The average car sells for $18,000. (a) Calculate the increase in the steel cost of each car and express it as a percentage of the car price. (b) Explain one effect on the car makers.
items.answer: (a) Extra cost = 1.2 × $800 × 25% = $240 per car, 1.33% of the price. (b) Higher costs reduce profit margins or force higher prices, making exports less competitive.
items.markingKey: (a) cost [1]; percentage [1] (b) [1] [3]

items.stem: Extract: Producers of smartphones in Marvona say they cannot compete with cheap imports from Selmaria, which they accuse of dumping. At the world price of $4, domestic firms supply 25 thousand units and consumers buy 77 thousand. The government is considering a tariff of $3 per unit, which would raise domestic output to 40 thousand and cut consumption to 65 thousand. Economists warn that Selmaria might retaliate against Marvona’s exports of bicycles. (a) Calculate the change in imports caused by the tariff. (b) Using a diagram, explain the effect of the tariff on consumers and domestic producers.
items.answer: (a) Before 52 thousand, after 25 thousand: a fall of 27 thousand. (b) Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Before 52 thousand, after 25 thousand: a fall of 27 thousand. [2] (b) Credit: Price rises from Pw to Pw + tariff; consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises; domestic output rises and imports fall; deadweight loss triangles. [4]
